# Math (Floats)(WIP)

Although negative integers turned out to be a challenge it's still reasonably easy to understand how some number of bits
can be mapped to an integer.  


```
// multiply.s - ARM64 macOS Assembly
// To assemble: as -o multiply.o multiply.s
// To link: ld -macosx_version_min 11.0.0 -o multiply multiply.o -lSystem

.global _main             // Entry point for macOS
.align 4

_main:
    // 1. Load the first constant into register d0
    adrp    x0, const1@PAGE
    ldr     d0, [x0, const1@PAGEOFF]

    // 2. Load the second constant into register d1
    adrp    x0, const2@PAGE
    ldr     d1, [x0, const2@PAGEOFF]

    // 3. Multiply: d2 = d0 * d1
    fmul    d2, d0, d1

    // 4. Convert result to integer for the exit code (optional, for demo)
    // 12.5 * 4 = 50. This will return 50 to the terminal.
    fcvtzs  w0, d2          

    // 5. Exit the program
    mov     x16, #1         // macOS syscall for exit
    svc     #0x80           // Invoke supervisor call

.section __DATA,__data
.align 3
const1: .double 12.5
const2: .double 4.0

```


Registers: We use d0, d1, and d2. These are 64-bit "Double" precision registers. If you wanted single precision (floats), you would use s0, s1, and s2.

Adrp/Ldr: ARM64 cannot load a 64-bit memory address in a single instruction. adrp finds the 4KB "page" where your data lives, and the ldr offset grabs the specific value.

fmul: This is the specific instruction for Floating-point Multiplication.

fcvtzs: This converts a Floating-point value to a Signed Integer (with truncation toward zero), which allows us to pass the result into w0 (the return register).
